attackPath.attacker: A local or workspace-adjacent attacker able to place an executable earlier in the operator's inherited PATH.
attackPath.impact: Production database credential disclosure, forged target attestation, and code execution with operator privileges.
preconditions: The operator runs the production cutover guard with the poisoned PATH.
The production database URL is supplied.
steps: Guard preserves inherited PATH.
Final validator launches bare node with the production URI in its environment.
Substitute captures the URI and exits successfully.

codeEvidence.code:
if ! safe_git -C "$REPO_ROOT" cat-file blob \
  "${REVIEWED_COMMIT}:${VALIDATOR_RELATIVE}" |
  GALLR_PRODUCTION_VALIDATION_PROJECT_REF="$PRODUCTION_REF" \
  GALLR_PRODUCTION_VALIDATION_DATABASE_URL="$PRODUCTION_DATABASE_URL" \
  NODE_OPTIONS='' NODE_PATH='' \
    node --input-type=module -
codeEvidence.explanation: The validator bytes are reviewed, but the interpreter receiving the production URI is selected from ambient PATH instead of the previously resolved TRUSTED_NODE.
codeEvidence.label: Credential-bearing bare node invocation

confidence.rationale: The source and test harness both show the final invocation uses PATH-selected node and receives the validation URI; live operator PATH contents are unknown.

originalCandidates.title: Production cutover passes the database URI to an inherited-PATH node
Production cutover passes the database URI to an inherited-PATH node

findings.remediation: Build an immutable absolute toolchain before accepting secrets, invoke the verified Node path for every validator, and bind the interpreter and dependencies to independently reviewed hashes or a non-writable installation. Add a regression proving a PATH-prepended node is never invoked.

rootCause.summary: A hardened workflow validates script bytes but does not bind the interpreter used for the secret-bearing step to immutable provenance.

findings.summary: The production target guard resolves a nominal trusted Node binary for one check, but the final credential-bearing validator invokes bare `node` through the inherited PATH. A substituted executable can steal the production PostgreSQL URI and forge successful attestation.
findings.title: Production cutover exposes the database URI to an inherited-PATH Node executable

validation.counterevidence: The validator blob is read from the reviewed commit and unrelated environment variables are cleared. An attacker still needs an executable earlier in the operator's PATH.
validation.evidence: SAFE_PATH copies inherited PATH; TRUSTED_NODE is resolved only in solo mode; the final call is bare node; tests deliberately prepend a node wrapper and observe the validation environment.
validation.method: Independent focused review plus parent source verification

attackPath.attacker: A gallery content author whose crafted text is approved and published.
attackPath.impact: Persistent JavaScript execution on the public gallr origin, including page tampering and access to origin-readable browser state.
preconditions: The crafted exhibition is published.
The static site rebuild includes it.
A visitor opens /map/.
steps: Submit a field containing a closing script tag and executable markup.
Publisher approves the draft.
Build embeds the literal terminator in the script island.
Browser executes the injected script.

codeEvidence.explanation: JSON escaping does not neutralize the HTML raw-text terminator, while `safe` suppresses template escaping.
codeEvidence.label: Unsafe JSON island sink

confidence.rationale: Two independent reviewers and direct source inspection establish controllable text, the raw-text sink, and lack of script-context escaping.

originalCandidates.title: Published catalogue fields can break out of the map JSON island
Published catalogue fields can break out of the map JSON island

findings.remediation: Use an HTML-script-safe JSON serializer that escapes at least `<`, `>`, `&`, U+2028, and U+2029; remove the generic `safe` filter; add `</script>` regression fixtures and deploy a restrictive CSP.

rootCause.summary: A generic JSON serializer is treated as safe for an HTML script-element context.

findings.summary: Published exhibition strings are JSON-serialized, marked safe, and embedded in a script raw-text element. A value containing `</script><script>…` terminates the data island and creates executable markup on the public map page.
findings.title: Published catalogue text can execute JavaScript through the map JSON island

validation.counterevidence: Owner drafts normally require staff publication and ordinary template interpolation is autoescaped; client rendering after parse uses textContent.
validation.evidence: mapData includes owner-controlled name, venue, address, and slug fields; owner validation only bounds strings; the template uses dump|safe; deployment config provides no compensating CSP.
validation.method: Independent focused review plus parent source verification

attackPath.attacker: A remote link sender or malicious installed app holding a valid Gallr account session.
attackPath.impact: Victim actions are performed in an attacker-controlled account and the victim's current app session is replaced.
preconditions: Victim opens or receives the crafted custom-scheme callback.
Attacker supplies valid tokens for the attacker's account.
steps: Attacker obtains their own Supabase session tokens.
Craft callback fragment with those tokens.
Victim device dispatches it to Gallr.
Gallr imports the attacker's session.

codeEvidence.code:
val accessToken = params["access_token"] ?: return
val refreshToken = params["refresh_token"] ?: return
supabaseClient.auth.importSession(
    UserSession(accessToken = accessToken, refreshToken = refreshToken, ...)
codeEvidence.explanation: Caller-provided tokens become the app session without a pending OAuth transaction or callback/state validation.
codeEvidence.label: Unbound implicit token import

confidence.rationale: Independent mobile and baseline reviews plus direct source inspection confirm the exported callback and unconditional implicit-token import.

preventiveControls: PKCE code exchange for the normal branch
Backend authorization remains tied to the imported account

originalCandidates.title: Unsolicited OAuth deep links can replace the mobile session
Unsolicited OAuth deep links can replace the mobile session

findings.remediation: Remove fragment-token import; accept only PKCE authorization-code callbacks; validate exact scheme/host/path and single-use state tied to a locally pending transaction; prefer verified HTTPS links.

rootCause.summary: Legacy implicit-flow support bypasses the PKCE transaction binding configured for normal login.

findings.summary: The shared callback handler accepts fragment access and refresh tokens without validating the callback origin, state, or a pending login transaction, then imports them as the current session.
findings.title: Unsolicited OAuth deep links can replace the mobile session

validation.counterevidence: The authorization-code branch uses PKCE and imported tokens grant only the attacker's own account, so this is session fixation/account confusion rather than victim-token theft.
validation.evidence: Android exports the browsable callback activity and both platforms forward URLs; the fragment branch has no scheme, host, state, or pending-flow check.
validation.method: Independent focused review plus parent source verification

attackPath.attacker: A later local user signing into a different account in the same running app process.
attackPath.impact: Disclosure of account A's bookmarked exhibitions to account B.
preconditions: Account A has bookmarks cached.
A signs out and B signs in without process restart.
The B refresh is pending or fails.
steps: The auth state switches to B.
UI subscribes to the unchanged cloud StateFlow.
A's exhibition IDs remain visible until successful refresh.

codeEvidence.code:
private val bookmarkedIds = MutableStateFlow<Set<String>>(emptySet())

fun observeBookmarkedIds(): Flow<Set<String>> = bookmarkedIds.asStateFlow()
codeEvidence.explanation: The cached set has no owner user ID and survives account changes for the repository lifetime.
codeEvidence.label: Global identity-free cloud cache

confidence.rationale: Direct source review confirms one global cache, auth-state routing to that cache for every authenticated user, and a retry failure path that leaves it unchanged.

preventiveControls: Process restart initializes an empty cache

originalCandidates.title: Bookmark cache exposes the previous account state after account switching
Bookmark cache exposes the previous account state after account switching

findings.remediation: Key cached state by user ID; synchronously publish empty/loading state on identity change; cancel and identity-check in-flight refreshes; clear account-scoped state on sign-out/deletion; test offline A-to-B transitions.

rootCause.summary: Account-private presentation state is cached by process rather than keyed and invalidated by authenticated user identity.

findings.summary: A process-global bookmark StateFlow is not keyed by user identity or cleared on auth transitions. Account B can observe account A's cached bookmarks while refresh is pending, and indefinitely if refresh fails.
findings.title: Bookmark cache exposes the previous account’s state after account switching

validation.counterevidence: Backend RLS prevents account B from querying A's rows; a successful refresh or process restart replaces/clears the stale set.
validation.evidence: SyncBookmarkRepository exposes the same cloud flow for every Authenticated state; refresh updates only after success and logs/returns after all retries fail.
validation.method: Independent focused review plus parent source verification

attackPath.attacker: A later user or guest with access to the same device.

steps: Logout clears only Auth state.
Server retains token and enabled subscriptions.
Publication fan-out continues to the device.

codeEvidence.explanation: Neither teardown path disables subscriptions, unregisters the push token, or rotates the persisted installation credential.

confidence.rationale: Focused mobile review traced client teardown, registration APIs, server binding, fan-out eligibility, and deletion semantics; parent confirmed the sign-out path and identity-conflict check.

originalCandidates.title: Sign-out and account deletion leave account-bound push subscriptions active
Sign-out and account deletion leave account-bound push subscriptions active

findings.remediation: Add an atomic authenticated revoke-installation operation; invoke it before sign-out/deletion and on identity changes; rotate local installation credentials; queue safe retry for offline cleanup; test A-to-B and deletion flows.

rootCause.summary: Remote notification registration lifecycle is not coupled to the owning authentication session lifecycle.

findings.summary: Authentication teardown only clears the Supabase session. Existing gallery alert installation, token, and enabled subscriptions remain registered, so the device can receive account A's follow-derived notifications after logout or account switching.

validation.counterevidence: Installation mutations require a high-entropy secret, cross-account takeover is rejected, users can manually disable individual alerts, and stale installations age out of some fan-out queries.

validation.method: Independent focused review plus parent source verification

attackPath.attacker: An unauthenticated network client able to supply an allowed Origin header.

steps: Submit unique exhibition_opened events backdated across ranking days.

codeEvidence.code:
where daily.event_name = 'exhibition_opened'
  and daily.occurred_on > ... - least(greatest(coalesce(p_days, 7), 7), 30)
...
order by sum(least(opens_by_day.opens, 20)) desc
codeEvidence.explanation: The public ordering trusts aggregates populated by unauthenticated clients and caps each day at a value well within one source's hourly quota.
codeEvidence.label: Ranking derived from caller-asserted anonymous events

confidence.rationale: Public-abuse review and direct source verification establish unauthenticated ingestion, backdating, quota/ranking math, and public consumption. Activation is feature-flag dependent.

originalCandidates.title: Anonymous mobile analytics can manipulate the public most-viewed ranking

findings.remediation: Do not use anonymous caller-asserted events for public ordering; use authenticated/server-observed signals or device-bound attestations; use receipt time; keep the kill switch off until integrity is established.
